title: More in imagination
hook: we suffer more in imagination than in reality

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Pacuvius, whose servants chanted: he has lived. Your line was a whole life. Today ends a week.

Your boss sends a message at four forty-five on a Friday: can we talk Monday? That's all. No subject. By Saturday morning you've lived through the whole meeting a dozen times. You've been criticized, demoted, let go. You've drafted your defense. Then on Monday it turns out she wanted to ask which conference room you like. Two days of suffering for something that never happened. Seneca's thirteenth letter catches this habit in a single sentence.
screen: `CAN WE TALK MONDAY?` → `A WHOLE WEEKEND OF DREAD.` → `MORE IN IMAGINATION.`

segments.voice: More things frighten us than actually hurt us, Seneca tells Lucilius. Then, in Gummere's translation: we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. Some things, he says, torment us more than they should. Some torment us before they should. And some torment us when they shouldn't at all. We exaggerate a trouble, we imagine one that isn't there, or we start suffering it early. So he gives a simple test. When a fear arrives, look at it closely. Is this trouble here now, or still in the future? If it's coming, is it certain, or only likely? And is it really an evil, or does it just feel like one? Much of what we dread, he says, never arrives. Between now and then, a lot can change. Look at this week: one is enough. All mine is with me. As if seen. Cato. We grew old together. A whole life. And now, more in the mind. One thread runs through them: much of what weighs on us lives in our heads, not in the world, and the world is often kinder than our forecasts. That's not a promise that nothing bad will happen. Seneca had real troubles, and some arrived. It's a habit: check the fear against the facts before you suffer it in full.
screen: `MORE FRIGHTENS US THAN HURTS US.` · `TOO MUCH, TOO SOON, OR FOR NOTHING.` · `HERE NOW? CERTAIN? REALLY BAD?` · `THE WEEK: CHECK THE FORECAST.` · then, large: `MORE IN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Bring one worry to mind and ask Seneca's questions slowly: is it happening now or later, certain or only possible, and how bad would it really be? Notice how much of the worry lived in the forecast. Then come back to your breath and your chair, where nothing has happened yet.
Opinione. Latin for in opinion: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact, so check each fear against the facts. Today's word.
Your line: more in the mind. Often the meeting is about conference rooms. Another week, done.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism question a fear before acting on it: is it present, is it certain, and is it truly bad?
